newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Glory or humiliation? Russian PM ponders new role.
newsitem.headline: Glory or humiliation? Russian PM ponders new role.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has survived a major government reshuffle, but he faces a change of role which offers at least as much chance of humiliation as glory.

President Boris Yeltsin's fierce criticism of the government's record and the naming of brilliant administrator Anatoly Chubais as first deputy prime minister in charge of the economy pose deep questions about Chernomyrdin's authority.

The president's motives are hazy enough for some political experts to say Chernomyrdin will be humiliated by playing second fiddle to Chubais, while others say he is being freed from everyday decision-making to groom him as Yeltsin's successor.
"Today decisions do not come down from the prime minister but depend to a much greater extent on Chubais," said Pavel Voshchanov, Yeltsin's ex-spokesman, in a television interview.
He said Chubais was likely to exercise his new powers by insisting that his own allies take important positions in the new cabinet, to be announced within the next week.
"If tomorrow we see what key positions people from Chubais' team take up, then we can say for sure that Chubais is in practice in charge of the cabinet," he said.
"What role will the prime minister play from then on? I think it will be a representative role and Prime Minister Chernomyrdin will become a shadow president."
Yeltsin, 66, has announced the cabinet shake-up to show he is back at the helm after months of illness and that he is intent on invigorating economic reforms.
He has made clear that almost all cabinet posts are up for grabs, except those of Chubais and Chernomyrdin.
Chernomyrdin has kept smiling through it all, humbly accepting Yeltsin's criticism and publicly backing Chubais' appointment, even if he risks being overshadowed by him.

Chubais, 41, has been given the role of turning around the economy because he is committed to reform and has a proven record as an organiser. He masterminded Yeltsin's re-election last July and has shone as his Kremlin chief of staff since then.
Chernomyrdin, a 58-year-old former gas industry chief, has by contrast a mixed record in four years as prime minister.
Hesitant where Chubais is decisive, and stolid while Chubais dazzles, Chernomyrdin is also a self-confessed mumbler who cannot match his new deputy's eloquence.
But Yeltsin had good reasons to retain his loyal premier and resist any urge to put Chubais formally in his place.

Chernomyrdin has worked out a modus vivendi with the opposition. But Chubais would be unlikely to be approved as prime minister by a parliament dominated by communists who loathe him for his earlier role in overseeing privatisation.

"He (Yeltsin) understood he must either sack the government and appoint someone who understands liberal reforms and how to carry them out, or reorganise the government, leave Chernomyrdin and appoint someone who understands liberal reforms and can work with Chernomyrdin," ex-acting prime minister Yegor Gaidar said.
He acknowledged the first option was unlikely and that Chubais fitted the bill for the second option.

The Kremlin is also looking for an eventual successor to Yeltsin to continue reforms and see off a challenge by former national security adviser Alexander Lebed, who is distrusted both in the Kremlin and by many opposition leaders.

There is no obvious successor. Chernomyrdin lacks charisma, but his chances of becoming president might improve if his government turned the economy round and if Chubais, who worked wonders for Yeltsin's campaign, were at his side.
His dismissal now would destroy any hope of him mounting a presidential campaign.
"Chernomyrdin remains Yeltsin's most likely successor in the next election. He has to be preserved as a political figure," said Otto Latsis, a commentator for the Izvestia newspaper.

The daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper said: "The prime minister's meekness is explained by a completely pragmatic understanding: he has been given guarantees that he will be Yeltsin's successor for the post of president."

Even if this is the case, Chernomyrdin can still be dismissed and disgraced as the ultimate sacrifice in any crisis. His job could next be under threat in nationwide wage protests planned for March 27.
"Chernomyrdin will be sacrificed only in a more critical situation, maybe if strikes and pressure mount on March 27," said political analyst Andrei Piontkowski.
"For now he is still needed as a stabilising element but he needs help (from Chubais) because alone he is not successful."
